component_records.title: Bid management, submission and clarification discipline
component_records.description: The bid team runs the proposal as a controlled process: all written questions, including requests for the missing attachments and the City's standard contract, are filed with accounting@colfax-ca.gov by the July 31, 2025 deadline so the City's August 14, 2025 responses can be folded into the final submission. The package is assembled to the RFP's required order and page limits, signed, and delivered as both a signed hard copy and a digital PDF so that it is physically in the City's hands before 4:00 PM PST on August 28, 2025; late proposals are not submitted because they would not be evaluated. The team also holds itself to the no-contact rule during evaluation and keeps the price at its most favorable terms, since clarification cannot change it.

component_records.title: Mobilization, project management and governance
component_records.description: A dedicated project manager and named technical staff are assigned at award, with a personnel management plan, a detailed implementation plan and timeline, and a weekly progress/budget/timeline meeting cadence with the City's Accounting and IT leads. The plan sequences work back from the July 1, 2026 go-live and is deliberately lightweight in its demands on City staff, reflecting a small client team. This component also carries the contractual and compliance obligations: acceptance of the RFP terms as contract conditions, the capped reimbursable and total-price structure, insurance and financial-condition certifications, and the 15-day notification of material changes to the certification. It also covers the bid team's availability for a virtual finalist interview on September 25, 2025 and the proposal-preparation cost position.

component_records.title: Hosted accounting and financial reporting platform
component_records.description: A cloud-hosted, subscription-based accounting and financial reporting system is configured for the City, covering Accounts Payable with 1099 filing, purchasing requisitions and purchase orders with approvals, Accounts Receivable, General Ledger, Payroll, Utility Billing and Business Licensing. The system captures financial transactions systematically, supports budgeting and forecasting, produces management and financial reports with data analysis for decision-making, and retains auditable records and documentation. Licensing is provisioned for the City's five current users with a defined path to add users later, and license types are identified by level of use. Account number customization is described in detail, including segment structure, length and the ability to change the chart of accounts without vendor intervention.

component_records.title: Account structure design and financial report writing
component_records.description: Working from the City's auditing and reporting requirements, the team recommends an account structure that supports auditable reporting and maps cleanly to the new system's chart of accounts, then builds the financial reports the City needs for decision-making and audit. Report writing is delivered as configured reports plus a documented report library the City can maintain, with power users trained to modify them. The design is reviewed with Accounting and IT before configuration is frozen so that audit trails and fund accounting conventions are preserved.

component_records.title: Data migration of five years of history
component_records.description: The prior five years of financial data are extracted from the City's current system, mapped, cleansed, validated and loaded into the new platform, with reconciliation reports signed off by Accounting before cutover. Migration runs in at least two trial loads so that balances, open items and history are proven before go-live. Cutover is scheduled to minimize downtime and operational disruption, with a documented rollback position and parallel running where the City requires it.

component_records.title: Training and change management
component_records.description: Training is tiered by license level and states for each tier whether it is delivered in person, virtually or as standard recordings. Power users receive personalized sessions and written manuals tailored to their modules; all staff receive at least one recorded training session plus a manual. A short change-management and communications plan prepares City staff for the new workflows, and training materials are handed over so the City can onboard future staff itself.

component_records.title: Post-implementation support and ongoing technical services
component_records.description: Twelve months of post-implementation support begins at go-live, delivered through a help desk and ticketing system that logs, prioritizes and reports on requests, with defined response targets and named escalation contacts. The same support continues into recurring services at annual renewal, with an account manager responsible for the City's relationship and periodic service reviews. Automated updates and proactive communications about software changes are issued ahead of each release, and annual e-filing for 1099s and W-2s is supported each filing season.

component_records.title: Price proposal and cost transparency
component_records.description: A single total price proposal is submitted on the City's pricing form, covering all services, materials, supplies and travel, with the implementation fee and recurring fees broken out in detail and license fees shown separately. Support costs are split between the implementation period and post-implementation, and an estimate is given for additional applications or third-party vendors. Reimbursable expenses are capped at a stated not-to-exceed amount, and the total price proposal is presented so that the services total and the reimbursable cap are unambiguous. The price is submitted at its most favorable terms on first submission, since clarification cannot change it.

component_records.title: Security, data protection and compliance evidence
component_records.description: Documentation is provided for the measures protecting the City's financial data and the secure access controls in place, covering encryption in transit and at rest, role-based access, multi-factor authentication, logging and monitoring, backup and recovery, and incident response. The evidence pack combines a narrative description with the platform's independent assurance reports and a completed Attachment G response, so the City can see both the controls and their independent validation. Hosting, data residency and any offshore support locations are disclosed in Attachment C, with written notice to the City if personnel later relocate outside the United States.

items.text: Conflicting submission methods: hard copy versus email. R041 requires one signed original proposal in hard copy while R045 requires the proposal and all attachments to be emailed to accounting@colfax-ca.gov by 4:00 PM PST on August 28, 2025, and R047 requires the hard copy to be physically received at the City address by the deadline. A bid that satisfies only one method risks being rejected as non-responsive, and a late courier delivery is fatal because late proposals are not evaluated. The proposed solution hedges by sending both, which costs duplication effort and still leaves the receipt risk on the physical copy. The two requirements are directly incompatible and the RFP does not resolve which governs; the consequence of guessing wrong is disqualification, but the dual-submission hedge reduces the chance of total failure.

items.text: July 1, 2026 go-live treated as firm but stated only as a goal. The RFP describes July 1, 2026 as the City's goal, not a contractual milestone, yet the proposed solution commits to it as a fixed date with mobilization in October 2025 and configuration, five-year migration, parallel testing and training all compressed into roughly nine months. If award slips, the standard contract is negotiated late, or the City's small staff cannot supply data and sign-offs on schedule, the date slips and the bidder carries the reputational and possibly contractual cost. The RFP also leaves the project start as 'soon after award' with no notice period. The schedule is tight for a full financial-system replacement with a five-year migration, and the start date depends on an award and negotiation timeline the RFP does not fix; the solution's own assumption converts an aspiration into a commitment.

Migration is a mandatory deliverable (R107) with no stated data profile, and the assumption that the legacy system exports cleanly is the bidder's, not the City's; migration overruns are a common cause of ERP go-live slippage.

With a bid team, subcontractors and reference clients all in play, an inadvertent contact with City staff could disqualify an otherwise strong proposal, and there is no stated process to self-report or cure it. The consequence is disqualification, which is severe, but the rule is clear enough that a disciplined bid team can comply; the residual risk comes from third parties the bidder does not fully control.
